Credit: RAJAAISYA/Science Photo Library/Getty Images Maintaining health can be hard work, particularly as we age. And many medical interventions currently available for older people are designed to manage discomfort or delay the decline of tissue function, rather than repair or reverse the effects of damage or disease.Meanwhile, life expectancy is steadily climbing over the years, and some countries are now facing the challenges of managing the medical needs of an increasing number of older people. Japan, for example, is one of the world’s ‘super-aged’ countries, with about 30% of its citizens aged 65 or older.“Bridging the gap between average life expectancy and healthy life expectancy has emerged as a paramount societal challenge,” says Kazuto Yamada, president and CEO of the regenerative medicine firm Japan Tissue Engineering Company (J-TEC), based near Nagoya.To illustrate, he cites the healthcare costs and reduced quality of life associated with mobility-impeding conditions such as osteoarthritis, which affects up to a third of older people.J-TEC and its parent company, the Teijin Group, hope to lead the way in exploring future regenerative therapies that achieve tissue repair by combining living cells with biocompatible materials. Any resulting clinical products might have the power to change the way conditions such as osteoarthritis are treated.“Regenerative medicine represents a paradigm shift from managing symptoms towards empowering a kind of autonomous functional recovery, potentially enabling older adults to maintain independent and active lives,” says Yamada.Osteoarthritis affects up to a third of older people globally. Researchers at J-TEC are exploring a new approach for treating it. Credit: Ijubaphoto/Getty Images Over the past 25 years, J-TEC has explored the possibility of a variety of cell-based therapies based on relatively simple assemblies of human cells. These include skin grafts for burn patients and sheets of cells for repairing defective or damaged corneal tissue in the eye that are grown in culture from a patient’s own cells.However, this approach might be less effective for more complex tissue repair efforts, where cells may fail to thrive or integrate with the surrounding host tissue in the absence of a supportive infrastructure.Active biomaterialsAs a solution, J-TEC and Teijin have been exploring a new combination of cells and novel materials. One approach combines J-TEC’s expertise in cell culture and tissue engineering with Teijin’s experience in the development of specialized polymers and other biocompatible materials. These materials are intended to establish an environment that guides and nurtures implanted cells, potentially enabling more seamless repair of damaged tissues.“Rather than viewing materials merely as passive delivery vehicles, Teijin designs active biomaterials engineered at the molecular level to interact synergistically with living cells,” says Hiroshi Kakidachi, CTO of the Regenerative Medicine and Implantable Medical Devices division at Teijin.Yamada says that the two partners bring complementary capabilities to the table. “J-TEC has accumulated extensive expertise in exploring regenerative-medicine methods with consistent quality despite the inherent biological variability of individual-patient-derived cells,” he explains. Meanwhile, Teijin has brought a diverse variety of medical devices into the clinical marketplace, navigating the complexities of safety testing, quality assurance and regulatory compliance.J-TEC has already commercialized one material that exemplifies the shared philosophy. Osteoarthritis occurs when the cartilage that buffers the joints erodes; this causes the bones to rub together, leading to pain and stiffness. Since the mid-1990s, clinicians have been treating the condition by implanting chondrocytes collected from the patient and cultured outside of the body into the affected joints1. This treatment was approved in US in 1997 for treating knee cartilage defects.Although often effective, the implantation of chondrocytes alone also has major limitations; for example, conventionally cultured cells tend to lose their chondrocyte identity, limiting their regenerative performance after implantation.New approachAs a solution, J-TEC explored scaling a technique developed in the mid-1990s by orthopedic surgeon Mitsuo Ochi and colleagues at Shimane Medical University in Japan2.In this approach, chondrocytes obtained from the patient are mixed with atelocollagen, a form of modified collagen that is less likely to trigger an immune response, says Katsura Sugawara, head of Cartilage Business at J-TEC, “forming a 3D construct, which is then trimmed to match the shape of the cartilage defect prior to implantation.”This robust, protein-based framework keeps the cells localized at the injury site after surgery while also creating an environment that preserves their cartilage-producing function.The resulting J-TEC autologous cultured cartilage (JACC) implants entered clinical use in Japan in 2013. Subsequent marketing surveillance studies have evaluated their effect on mobility and quality of life3.The company has since explored a newer iteration of these implants, which incorporates an additional collagen membrane to cover the graft after implantation. The clinical utility and safety of JACC used with the collagen membrane was evaluated using post-marketing surveillance data4.Diverse applicationsTeijin and J-TEC are now exploring various avenues for future tissue-engineering efforts. One of these are as alternatives to animal testing for drug-development purposes.Kazuto Yamada of J-TEC and Yuji Nakahara and Hiroshi Kakidachi of Teijin having a discussion while examining a model of a knee joint. Credit: TeijinJ-TEC already manufactures relatively simple epithelial-cell-based models of human skin and eye tissue for such applications, which are listed in OECD guidelines for skin sensitization testing.Yamada says the company is actively engaged in developing surrogates for a range of other tissues as well. “Looking ahead, J-TEC expects these technologies to find broader applications in the evaluation of food products, medical materials and other industries requiring safety assessment,” he says. In light of the success of its own regenerative medicine products, the company is also expanding into contract product development and manufacturing.And in the context of future clinical innovations, the researchers believe there are abundant opportunities to develop patient-tailored biomaterial-based scaffolds that better replicate natural biological environments. For example, by combining Teijin’s precision biomaterial and scaffold technologies with J-TEC’s expertise in cell culture and 3D tissue engineering, they plan to create more complex, functional tissues for long-term graft viability.“Integrating biocompatible scaffolds with techniques for the precise spatial arrangement of multiple cell types has the potential to create biomimetic environments that offers a new approach to tissue fabrication,” says Kakidachi.In parallel, Teijin researchers are exploring sophisticated computational strategies that allow them to simulate the behaviour of different combinations of cells and scaffolds to find the best design for a given tissue site and indication, thereby accelerating the clinical development process.Although much work remains to be done, Yamada is enthusiastic about the future of the field. “Our greatest expectation is to see regenerative medicine become not merely a form of advanced or specialized care, but a standard treatment option that is widely accessible to patients,” he says.
